metadata.dsm5_code: F06.33 (with manic features), F06.34 (with mixed features)
metadata.icd10_code: F19.94 (other psychoactive substance-induced mood disorder, with manic symptoms)

aeo.what_is: Manic or hypomanic symptoms triggered by drugs, alcohol, or medications that resolve when the substance is stopped.

content.temporal_criteria: Symptoms must develop during or soon after substance intoxication, withdrawal, or medication exposure. The timeline linking symptom onset to the substance is critical. Symptoms typically resolve within days to weeks after stopping the substance, though some may persist longer. If symptoms continue more than a month after full cessation, consider a primary bipolar disorder.

confused_with: Primary Bipolar I or II Disorder — the key distinction is whether episodes occur independently of substance use. If someone has manic episodes that happen when they're not using substances, or that started before substance use began, it's likely primary bipolar disorder. Substances may worsen existing bipolar, but they're not the sole cause.

Substance Intoxication — simple intoxication (high energy from cocaine, euphoria from cannabis) is different from a full manic syndrome. Substance-induced bipolar requires meeting manic/hypomanic criteria with elevated mood, decreased sleep need, grandiosity, risky behavior, etc., not just being 'high.'
Delirium — delirium involves fluctuating consciousness, disorientation, and confusion during intoxication or withdrawal. Substance-induced mania has clear consciousness with mood elevation.
ADHD — chronic hyperactivity and impulsivity from ADHD differ from acute manic symptoms during substance use. The timeline and episodic nature help distinguish.
Personality Disorder — impulsivity and emotional dysregulation from personality disorders are lifelong patterns, while substance-induced mania is acute and tied to substance exposure.
misdiagnosis_explained.clarifying_factors: Detailed substance use timeline (what, when, how much); history of mood symptoms before substance use; collateral from family/friends about baseline functioning; urine toxicology; medical record review for medication changes; symptoms resolving after cessation; distinguishing unmasking of latent bipolar disorder versus pure substance effect.
misdiagnosis_explained.timeline_differences: Primary bipolar has episodes that occur without substance use. Substance-induced mania occurs only during or soon after exposure and resolves with abstinence. Simple intoxication resolves within hours; substance-induced mania lasts days to weeks after exposure ends.
misdiagnosis_explained.impairment_differences: Both cause severe impairment during the episode. The difference is etiology. Substance-induced mania is expected to resolve fully with abstinence, while primary bipolar requires long-term mood stabilization even without substances.

description.overview: Substance/Medication-Induced Bipolar and Related Disorder is characterized by a prominent and persistent mood disturbance—elevated, expansive, or irritable mood—with or without depressive symptoms, that develops during or soon after substance intoxication, withdrawal, or exposure to a medication. The mood symptoms are temporally related to the substance/medication and not better explained by a primary bipolar disorder.
what_it_can_look_like_in_real_life: A 30-year-old with no psychiatric history starts high-dose prednisone for an autoimmune flare. Within days, he's sleeping only three hours, talking rapidly, making grandiose plans to start a business, and irritable when questioned. His symptoms resolve within two weeks of tapering the steroid.

A 25-year-old uses cocaine heavily for a week and develops euphoria, boundless energy, racing thoughts, and risky sexual behavior. She doesn't sleep for three days. After stopping cocaine and abstaining for two weeks, her mood returns to normal.

A 50-year-old on a new antidepressant (without a mood stabilizer) suddenly becomes hypomanic—needing less sleep, starting multiple projects, talking nonstop, and spending impulsively. Her doctor stops the antidepressant, and within a week she's back to baseline.

A 35-year-old with no mood disorder history takes anabolic steroids for bodybuilding. He becomes aggressively irritable, hypersexual, and grandiose, convinced he's invincible. His family convinces him to stop the steroids, and his mood stabilizes within a month.

A 40-year-old starts a stimulant medication for ADHD and within days feels 'too good'—euphoric, overly talkative, impulsive. His psychiatrist recognizes drug-induced hypomania, stops the stimulant, and his mood normalizes.

A 28-year-old taking corticosteroids for asthma develops severe insomnia, irritability, and impulsive spending. She feels 'wired' and can't sit still. After her pulmonologist tapers the dose, her mood and sleep return to normal.
common_reactions_to_diagnosis: Relief that the symptoms are caused by a substance and not a chronic mental illness.
Concern about whether it will happen again if they're exposed to the same substance or medication.
Confusion about why a medication or substance caused such extreme mood changes.
Fear that they've 'broken' their brain or triggered a permanent condition.
Frustration if the substance was medically necessary (like steroids) and they had no choice.
Worry about whether they actually have underlying bipolar disorder that the substance unmasked.
Hope that staying off the substance will prevent future episodes.

content.diagnostic_criteria: A. Prominent, persistent disturbance in mood predominated by elevated, expansive, or irritable mood, with or without depressive symptoms. B. Evidence from history, physical exam, or labs that (1) symptoms developed during or soon after intoxication, withdrawal, or medication exposure; and (2) the substance/medication is capable of producing such symptoms. C. Not better explained by an independent bipolar disorder (e.g., symptoms preceded onset of use, persist >1 month after cessation, or have other non-substance cause). D. Symptoms do not occur exclusively during delirium. E. Causes clinically significant distress or impairment.
content.prevalence: Unknown precise prevalence; occurs in context of stimulant, corticosteroid, or antidepressant use; higher risk in individuals with mood disorder vulnerability.
content.age_of_onset: Can occur at any age depending on timing of exposure; often emerges during early or middle adulthood when substance use or medical treatment is common.
content.prognosis: Usually resolves within days to weeks after cessation of substance/medication, but may unmask or trigger chronic bipolar disorder in predisposed individuals. Recurrence likely with re-exposure.

circuitry: Acute dysregulation of prefrontal-limbic circuits, including amygdala hyperactivation and reduced prefrontal control.
Alterations in reward pathways (ventral striatum) during substance intoxication.
neurochemistry: Excess dopaminergic transmission with stimulants and certain medications.
Glucocorticoid effects on limbic circuitry with corticosteroid-induced mania.
neurobiology.genetic_environmental: Underlying bipolar vulnerability increases risk; stress, sleep deprivation, and high-dose/prolonged medication exposure are contributing factors.

history_psychosocial: Detailed substance use and medication exposure timeline relative to symptom onset.
Past psychiatric history and family history of mood disorders.
Psychosocial stressors, supports, and functional impact.
medical_assessment: Physical and neurologic exam to rule out other causes.
Laboratory tests for toxicology, metabolic profile, thyroid function, and relevant medication levels.
standardized_measures: Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS) for mania severity.
Mood Disorder Questionnaire (MDQ) to screen for bipolar spectrum.
risk_stratification: Evaluate suicide risk, risk-taking behaviors, aggression, and potential for harm during intoxication or withdrawal.
differential_diagnosis: Primary bipolar I or II disorder
Substance intoxication or withdrawal without mood disorder
evaluation.team_and_process: Coordinate with addiction specialists, psychiatry, and prescribing clinicians; ensure safe detoxification and monitoring.

manic_hypomanic: Flight of ideas or racing thoughts

severity_levels.mild: Few symptoms beyond diagnostic threshold; mild functional impairment.
severity_levels.moderate: Symptoms and impairment between mild and severe; safety concerns manageable.
severity_levels.severe: Marked functional impairment, high-risk behaviors, or severe agitation/psychosis.

biological: Personal or family history of bipolar disorder
Neurobiological sensitivity to dopaminergic or glucocorticoid effects
environmental: Easy access to substances or medications with manic potential

impact_on_life.school_work: Erratic attendance, reduced performance, impulsive work decisions.
impact_on_life.social: Conflict, legal issues, or financial consequences due to risky behavior.
impact_on_life.medical: Poor adherence to medical treatment; worsening of comorbid conditions.
impact_on_life.emotional: Shame, regret, and distress after episodes.

comorbidities: Medical conditions requiring corticosteroids or dopaminergic agents

psychotherapy: Psychoeducation on substance effects and relapse prevention.
CBT for mood stabilization and coping strategies.
medications: Acute mania: antipsychotics (e.g., haloperidol, olanzapine, risperidone) or mood stabilizers (e.g., lithium, valproate).
Taper or discontinue offending medication/substance when possible.
Avoid antidepressants without mood stabilizer if bipolar risk present.
care_coordination: Collaboration between prescriber, psychiatry, and addiction services.
Regular monitoring for recurrence with re-exposure.

treatment_goals: Achieve full remission of substance-induced mood symptoms.
Prevent recurrence via abstinence or medication changes.
Address underlying bipolar vulnerability if present.
missed_diagnosis_factors: Failure to link symptom onset to substance/medication exposure.
Assuming symptoms are purely due to intoxication without mood disorder.
Not recognizing unmasking of latent bipolar disorder.
overdiagnosis_factors: Labeling primary bipolar disorder as substance-induced without adequate history.
Misattributing mood changes from withdrawal as mania.
warning_signs: Escalating risky behavior or aggression during substance use.
Emergence of psychosis or suicidal ideation.
self_help_strategies: Engage in recovery programs and peer support.
Track mood changes relative to medication/substance use.

adolescence: Often linked to stimulant or anabolic steroid use; may impair academic and social development.
adulthood: Commonly related to prescription medications (e.g., corticosteroids) or illicit stimulants.
older_adults: Medication-induced cases more common; polypharmacy increases risk.

first_person_statements: I'd never felt anything like it—I was on top of the world, unstoppable, and didn't need sleep. Then I found out it was the prednisone.
I thought I was losing my mind. My doctor explained it was the cocaine, and once I stopped, I went back to normal. It was terrifying.
The antidepressant flipped a switch in me. I went from depressed to hypomanic in days. Stopping it was the right call.
I didn't realize steroids could do that. I was aggressive, impulsive, and felt invincible. My family was scared, and so was I.
The scariest part was not knowing if I'd go back to normal. Thankfully, once the drug cleared my system, I was myself again.
I'm grateful it was substance-induced and not lifelong bipolar disorder, but it makes me cautious about what I put in my body now.

comparisons: It's like someone turned up all your dials to maximum—energy, mood, impulsivity—because of a chemical you took, and turning off that chemical brings everything back down.
Imagine your brain's accelerator getting stuck because of a drug, making you speed through life uncontrollably until the drug wears off and the accelerator releases.
Think of it as a temporary software glitch caused by introducing a foreign code (the substance)—once you remove the code, the system reboots to normal.
It's like a firework that's set off by the substance: bright, explosive, chaotic, and then it fizzles out when the substance is gone.

faqs.question: How do I know if it's substance-induced or primary bipolar disorder?
faqs.answer: The key is timeline. If manic symptoms only occur during or shortly after substance use and resolve with abstinence, it's likely substance-induced. If you've had manic episodes without any substance use, it's primary bipolar disorder. Sometimes substances unmask underlying bipolar vulnerability.

faqs.question: Will I develop bipolar disorder permanently after substance-induced mania?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Most people return to baseline after the substance is cleared. However, in some cases, the episode may unmask a latent bipolar disorder, and future episodes can occur without substances. Close monitoring is important.

faqs.question: What substances and medications commonly cause mania?
faqs.answer: Stimulants (cocaine, amphetamines, ADHD medications), corticosteroids (prednisone, dexamethasone), antidepressants (especially without mood stabilizers), anabolic steroids, certain antiviral medications, and high doses of caffeine or energy drinks can trigger mania in vulnerable individuals.

faqs.question: How long does it take for symptoms to go away after stopping the substance?
faqs.answer: Most symptoms improve within days to weeks after stopping the substance. Stimulants and short-acting drugs resolve faster (days), while medications with longer half-lives (like corticosteroids) may take weeks to fully clear.

faqs.question: Do I need long-term treatment?
faqs.answer: If it's purely substance-induced and you have no history of bipolar disorder, long-term treatment may not be needed once the substance is out of your system. However, you may need short-term medication (antipsychotics or mood stabilizers) to manage acute symptoms. Avoid the triggering substance in the future.

faqs.question: Can I ever use that substance or medication again?
faqs.answer: It depends. If it was a medication you need for a medical condition (like steroids for asthma or autoimmune disease), your doctor may try lower doses or alternatives, and psychiatric medication may be used preventively. If it was a recreational drug, avoiding it is strongly recommended.

faqs.question: What if the medication is medically necessary (like steroids)?
faqs.answer: Your medical team can try the lowest effective dose, shorter courses, or alternative treatments. A psychiatrist can prescribe mood stabilizers or atypicals preventively to reduce the risk of mania during steroid treatment.

faqs.question: Can substance-induced mania be dangerous?
faqs.answer: Yes. Like primary mania, it can involve risky behavior (spending, sexual activity, aggression), impaired judgment, and in severe cases, psychosis or violence. Immediate treatment is important to ensure safety.

faqs.question: What should I do if I think I'm becoming manic from a medication?
faqs.answer: Contact your prescribing doctor and psychiatrist immediately. Don't stop medications abruptly (especially steroids or antidepressants) without guidance, but urgent evaluation is needed to adjust treatment and prevent escalation.

faqs.question: Can alcohol or cannabis cause mania?
faqs.answer: Heavy alcohol or cannabis use can contribute to mood instability, but they more commonly cause intoxication or withdrawal symptoms rather than full manic episodes. Stimulants and steroids are more typical culprits.

faqs.question: Will I need to be hospitalized?
faqs.answer: If symptoms are severe (psychosis, extreme agitation, dangerous behavior, inability to care for yourself), hospitalization may be needed for safety and stabilization. Milder cases can be managed outpatient with close monitoring.

faqs.question: Can stress or lack of sleep make it worse?
faqs.answer: Yes. Sleep deprivation and stress can worsen substance-induced mania, just like primary mania. Prioritizing sleep, reducing stimulation, and managing stress are important during and after the episode.

faqs.question: What if I have a family history of bipolar disorder?
faqs.answer: A family history increases your risk. Substance-induced mania may be more likely to unmask underlying bipolar vulnerability in people with genetic risk. Close monitoring and avoiding triggering substances is especially important.

faqs.question: Can this happen with over-the-counter medications or supplements?
faqs.answer: Yes. High doses of caffeine, energy drinks, diet pills, and certain supplements (like St. John's Wort combined with antidepressants) can trigger mood elevation in susceptible individuals.

faqs.question: How can I prevent this from happening again?
faqs.answer: Avoid the substance that triggered the episode. If you need medical treatment that could cause mania, work with your doctors to use preventive psychiatric medications. Maintain good sleep, avoid other mood-destabilizing substances, and monitor for early warning signs.

real_life_examples.person: A 45-year-old woman with lupus was started on high-dose prednisone during a disease flare. Within a week, she developed pressured speech, decreased need for sleep, and impulsive online shopping, spending thousands of dollars. Her rheumatologist collaborated with psychiatry to taper the prednisone and start olanzapine. Her symptoms fully resolved within two weeks, and she hasn't had another episode.

A 28-year-old man with no psychiatric history used cocaine heavily for five days straight. He became euphoric, grandiose, and convinced he could start a tech company overnight. He didn't sleep and engaged in risky sexual behavior. After being brought to the ER by friends, he was detoxed and observed. His mood returned to baseline after 10 days of abstinence. He's now in recovery and symptom-free.

A 50-year-old woman was started on an SSRI for depression without a mood stabilizer. Within days, she became hypomanic—starting multiple projects, staying up late, talking rapidly, and irritable. Her psychiatrist recognized antidepressant-induced hypomania, stopped the SSRI, and started lamotrigine. She stabilized within a week and is now maintained on a mood stabilizer alone.

A 35-year-old bodybuilder took anabolic steroids and developed severe irritability, aggression, grandiosity, and hypersexuality. His family intervened after he got into a fight and made reckless financial decisions. He stopped the steroids and was treated with risperidone for two weeks. His mood normalized within a month, and he avoids steroids now.

A 40-year-old man started a stimulant for ADHD and within three days felt 'too good'—euphoric, overly talkative, and impulsive. His psychiatrist immediately stopped the stimulant and switched to a non-stimulant (atomoxetine). His mood returned to normal within days, and the non-stimulant controlled his ADHD without mood side effects.

content.when_to_seek_help: Seek immediate help if manic symptoms, risky behavior, psychosis, or suicidal thoughts emerge during or after substance/medication use.

positive_factors: Rapid identification and discontinuation of offending agent
Strong social support and treatment adherence
